summary: For ages 9–10, solve comparison, sum and difference problems from line graphs. Read each point using both axes and the labelled scale; distinguish the highest observed value from the largest increase over equal time intervals. Use temperatures for reading and differences, and quantities that can meaningfully be added, such as monthly rainfall totals, for sum problems. Interpolated temperatures are estimates under a stated straight-line assumption, not additional measurements. Joining monthly rainfall totals does not reveal rainfall on intermediate dates.
misconceptions: Graph-as-picture: reading the line's silhouette as a literal picture of the situation (a rising-then-falling temperature line 'is a hill/mountain', or a distance-time line read as the route travelled) rather than as a quantity plotted against time

Slope-height / height-for-difference confusion: when asked how much a quantity changed, naming the highest point rather than the steepest segment; treating a higher point as 'faster' or 'more increase'
Treating a line-based estimate as an exact unmeasured observation, or refusing any estimate because only the plotted points were measured.
Accepting or interpreting a joined line for categorical data (favourite pet) as if it showed a trend, or reading a scaled axis by counting squares rather than by the scale interval

activities.title: Read values and estimate between temperature observations
steps: Use a temperature-over-a-week line graph with observations at the same time each day and equal daily spacing. Slide a ruler, crosshair or finger along a segment to read a straight-line estimate between observations.

Slide between Monday and Tuesday and say aloud the values the line passes through — e.g. 14, 15, 16 degrees — noticing that the line gives estimated in-between values, not only the measured values at the plotted dots.

For each point, trace it back to BOTH axes: finger on the point, drop straight down to the time axis to read the day, then go back to the point and slide horizontally across to the value axis to read the temperature; say the paired coordinate.
Use a 'find the difference' move: mark two points and read the vertical gap between them (e.g. the rise from Tuesday to Wednesday).
Take on the challenge 'Which day did it warm up the MOST?' — then check whether the warmest day (tallest point) is the same as, or different from, the day of the steepest climb.
activities.insight: On this temperature graph, plotted points are observations and the connecting segments provide straight-line estimates between them. Compare rises over equal daily intervals to distinguish change from the temperature at a point.

activities.title: Separate HEIGHT from CHANGE on one graph
steps: On a single temperature line graph, answer 'Which day was warmest?' (height) and 'Which day did it warm up the most?' (steepest rise) — treat them as two different questions.
Draw a small vertical arrow for the change between each pair of consecutive days, pointing up for a rise and down for a fall, then compare the lengths of the upward arrows to find the biggest rise.
Justify your 'warmed up the most' answer by saying how far the line climbed across that one day, not by which point is highest.

Try a tricky case: a graph where a huge jump happens early in the week and the highest point is reached later by only a small rise, so the tallest point and the steepest segment are clearly on different days — identify each.
activities.insight: A higher observed temperature is not the same as a bigger increase. Over these equal one-day intervals, the largest rise has the steepest rising segment; with unequal intervals, compare changes and rates separately.

activities.title: Read the data, between the data, and beyond the data
steps: Read the data: lift a single value straight off a marked point (e.g. the warmest day's temperature).

Read between the data: compare two observed values, find their difference, and combine values only where the quantity makes a meaningful total, such as rainfall totals for March and May. Do not add daily temperatures as if they were a total temperature. On a temperature line graph, separately estimate an intermediate value under the straight-line assumption.

Read beyond the data: hide the final plotted day (e.g. Friday on a Monday-to-Friday graph), predict and place it from the earlier trend, then reveal the real value and compare — discuss why the prediction may differ.
Each time, name which kind of reading you are doing: reading a value, reading between, or predicting.
activities.insight: Graph comprehension has a progression — you must read a value before you can compare, combine or find differences between values, and only then predict or infer — and naming which you are doing clarifies the task.

activities.title: When should data be joined into a line? Continuous vs categorical
steps: Compare a genuine time-series (temperature across days) with categorical data (favourite fruit) and decide which should be drawn as a joined line and which should not.
Run a finger along a temperature segment, naming the estimates it passes through ('the line estimates about 15 here'); distinguish these from temperatures actually measured at the plotted points.
Explain why joining 'favourite fruit' counts into a line would be meaningless — there is no continuous quantity between the categories.
activities.insight: A line joining temperature observations can show a trend and support estimates under an explicit interpolation assumption. Joining unordered fruit categories does not create a meaningful intermediate category; use bars for those counts.

activities.title: Confront the graph-as-picture habit
steps: If you catch yourself describing the line as 'a hill' or 'the route it travelled', cover the whole line and expose one point at a time.
For each exposed point, answer 'What does THIS point tell us?' and trace it to both axes, reading a day and its temperature.
Re-read the whole graph as a set of day/temperature pairs rather than a shape or a scene.
activities.insight: The line is a quantity plotted against time, not a literal picture of the event; each point is a paired coordinate, and the overall shape summarises how the value changed, not a landscape.

activities.title: Check questions and reading the scale correctly
steps: Answer scorable items: choose the warmest day; estimate an intermediate temperature off a marked line (a sensible range is accepted); fill in 'the difference between March and May rainfall is ___ mm'; order months by rainfall.
Include one item that pairs 'highest point' against 'biggest rise' so you must distinguish height from change.
Before reporting any value, ask 'How much is each square worth here?' and label the scale interval, then read by the scale — not by counting squares as if each were one unit.
activities.insight: Targeted questions can check your reading skill, but you must read values by the axis scale interval, not by counting grid squares.

checkQuestion: Give an equally spaced line graph of temperatures recorded at noon: Monday 12°C, Tuesday 16°C, Wednesday 18°C, Thursday 17°C, Friday 19°C. Ask the learner to (1) read the warmest day and value, (2) calculate the Tuesday-to-Wednesday change, and (3) identify the interval with the largest rise. (4) Ask for the estimated temperature halfway between Tuesday noon and Wednesday noon, explicitly assuming straight-line change. (5) Then show a line graph of monthly rainfall totals (January 20 mm, February 35 mm, March 25 mm); ask for January plus March and the February–January difference. (6) Return to the temperature graph and ask what the falling Wednesday-to-Thursday segment means. Watch the reading and calculations without supplying the answers.
checkAnswer: Friday is warmest at 19°C; Tuesday to Wednesday rises by 2°C; Monday to Tuesday has the largest daily rise, 4°C, although Friday is highest. Halfway between Tuesday noon and Wednesday noon the straight-line estimate is 17°C; the actual unmeasured temperature may differ. January plus March rainfall is 45 mm and February exceeds January by 15 mm. Wednesday to Thursday falls by 1°C, meaning the temperature decreased (it got colder), not that something went downhill. Both traces start at the plotted point: vertically to time and horizontally to value. Do not total daily temperatures or interpolate monthly rainfall totals as rainfall at an intermediate date.
